summary: We developed Space Survivor, an educational space-survival game for ages 7 and up that runs on phone and laptop. Players choose a destination (Moon or Mars), prepare supplies, launch with real rocket-separation timing, and then survive on the surface by balancing six resources: oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation shielding and rest, while reacting to space events such as solar storms and dust storms. It addresses the challenge by turning real NASA data and mission records into decisions players must make, and by explaining after every mission the real reason behind each constraint. Solar-flare strength is fetched live from NASA DONKI, and every other number is labelled as a real reference value or a game simplification. It matters because learners understand why space life support is hard by experiencing the trade-offs, not by memorising facts.
details:
What it does and how it works: Space Survivor is an educational space-survival game for ages 7 and up. The player picks a destination (Moon or Mars) and a vehicle, prepares supplies, launches by pressing a button at each rocket separation (timing modelled on real mission records), lands, and survives by balancing six resources (oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation shield and rest) while reacting to space events such as solar storms, dust storms and meteoroids. Every choice trades one resource against another. After each mission a "What you learned" screen names the tightest resource and explains the real constraint behind it, and a "Science behind the game" screen labels every data point as Live NASA data, Real reference value, or Game simplification. Only the strength of solar flares is fetched live (NASA DONKI); everything else is reference data or clearly marked simplification.

Benefits and intended impact: Learners experience why life support in space is hard instead of memorising facts, and they learn to tell real data from simplified game numbers. We intend it as a classroom and home tool that makes NASA science approachable for children and adults, in Arabic and English. We have not yet measured learning outcomes; the next step is a school pilot.

Tools and technologies: HTML5 Canvas, WebGL and JavaScript in a single self-contained file; Capacitor (Android app); Electron (Windows app); GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions (hosting and automatic builds); NASA Open APIs (DONKI); Playwright for automated testing; AI assistance. No special hardware is needed: it runs on phones with touch controls and on laptops with the keyboard.

Creativity: the project turns a mission into a set of honest trade-offs, adds a telescope that shows real sky objects with real NASA spacecraft imagery, a mystery quest, and a training mode, and builds scientific honesty into the interface instead of hiding simplifications.

Factors we considered: scientific accuracy and labelling of what is real versus simplified; accessibility (touch and keyboard play, adjustable text size, screen-reader labels, reduced motion); privacy and child safety (progress stays on the device, the microphone is optional and requires consent, and under-13s are told to ask a parent); working on phones, laptops and offline; Arabic and English; and not implying NASA endorsement.
